nodes.label: Cyrus II founds the empire
nodes.full: Cyrus united the Persians and Medes, overthrew his grandfather Astyages of Media (c.550 BC), conquered Lydia under Croesus (c.547 BC), and took Babylon without a siege in 539 BC. He died in 530 BC campaigning against the Massagetae on the empire's eastern steppe frontier.
nodes.src: Cyrus Cylinder (British Museum ME 90920); Nabonidus Chronicle (BM 35382); Herodotus, Histories 1.46–214.

nodes.label: Cyrus conquers Media, Lydia, Babylon
nodes.full: In a single decade Cyrus overturned the political map of the Near East: he took Ecbatana from his grandfather Astyages (c.550 BC), captured Sardis from Croesus of Lydia (c.547 BC), and entered Babylon without a fight after Nabonidus's army collapsed at Opis (539 BC).
nodes.src: Nabonidus Chronicle (BM 35382); Cyrus Cylinder (BM 90920); Herodotus, Histories 1.75–91, 1.153–214.

nodes.label: Cyrus Cylinder and Marduk
nodes.full: Composed by or for Babylon's own priesthood, the Cyrus Cylinder casts Cyrus as the choice of the god Marduk, sent to end Nabonidus's neglect of the cult and restore proper temple worship — royal legitimation expressed entirely in the conquered city's own religious idiom.
nodes.src: Cyrus Cylinder (British Museum ME 90920).

nodes.label: Cyrus edict for Jerusalem
nodes.full: The Book of Ezra records a decree of Cyrus authorising the Judean exiles in Babylon to return home and rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem, funded in part from the royal treasury — consistent with the general policy of restoring local cults and returning displaced peoples that the Cyrus Cylinder claims for Babylon itself.
nodes.src: Ezra 1:1–4, 6:3–5; Cyrus Cylinder (BM 90920) for the parallel general policy.

nodes.label: Return and Second Temple
nodes.full: Following Cyrus's decree, groups of Judean exiles returned to Jerusalem under Sheshbazzar and later Zerubbabel; the rebuilt Temple was completed and dedicated in the sixth year of Darius I, 516 BC, after delays the Book of Ezra attributes to local opposition and a change of Persian administration.
nodes.src: Ezra 1–6; Book of Haggai (dated to Darius's second year, 520 BC).

nodes.label: Tomb of Cyrus
nodes.full: Cyrus's tomb — a gabled stone chamber raised on a stepped plinth, standing apart from the palace terraces — combines Elamite platform-building with Anatolian and Mesopotamian elements, an early statement of the composite visual language the dynasty would use throughout its architecture.
nodes.src: Pasargadae excavations, David Stronach (1961–63); Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 6.29 (Alexander's visit and restoration of the tomb).

nodes.label: Steppe frontier economy
nodes.full: Along the empire's northeastern satrapies, Saka and Massagetae pastoral-nomadic groups were managed through tribute in horses and livestock and negotiated frontier arrangements rather than direct conquest — Cyrus's own death campaigning against the Massagetae shows the limits Persian military and fiscal power met at this frontier.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 1.201–216; Achaemenid administrative texts on Saka tribute (Persepolis Fortification Archive).

nodes.label: Cambyses II
nodes.full: Cambyses defeated Pharaoh Psamtik III at Pelusium in 525 BC and was crowned Pharaoh at Memphis, founding Egypt's Twenty-Seventh (Persian) Dynasty. He died in 522 BC on the road home from Egypt, as news reached him of a usurpation at the heart of the empire.
nodes.src: Udjahorresnet inscription (Vatican Museums, Naophorous statue); Behistun Inscription (DB) §11; Herodotus, Histories 3.1–38.

nodes.label: Battle of Pelusium
nodes.full: Cambyses defeated Pharaoh Psamtik III's army at Pelusium on the eastern Delta frontier, opening the road to Memphis and ending Egypt's Twenty-Sixth (Saite) Dynasty as an independent power.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 3.10–13; Polyaenus, Strategemata 7.9 (the cats-as-shields tradition, treated with source-critical caution).

nodes.label: Apis bulls of Memphis
nodes.full: Herodotus claims Cambyses stabbed the sacred Apis bull in a fit of impiety, but a stela from the Serapeum at Saqqara records an Apis burial performed and inscribed in Cambyses's own name in 524 BC — archaeological evidence that directly contradicts the hostile Greek literary tradition about Persian rule in Egypt.
nodes.src: Serapeum Apis stela of Year 6 of Cambyses (Louvre); Herodotus, Histories 3.27–29, for the tradition it contradicts.

nodes.label: Bardiya (Gaumata)
nodes.full: For roughly seven months a man Darius's own inscription names as the magus Gaumata ruled as Bardiya, claiming to be Cyrus's surviving son. Darius's account — the only detailed source — calls him an impostor and the dead prince's murderer; modern historians note this is exactly the story a usurper would need to tell, and the truth beneath it cannot be fully recovered.
nodes.src: Behistun Inscription (DB) §§10–13; Herodotus, Histories 3.61–79.

nodes.label: Magi as ritual specialists
nodes.full: Herodotus names the Magi as one of the Median tribes and describes their distinctive funerary practice — exposing the dead to birds and dogs before burial — alongside their role interpreting royal dreams and officiating at sacrifice, evidence for a specialised priesthood distinct from the general population's practice.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 1.101, 1.140.

nodes.label: Darius I
nodes.full: Darius killed Gaumata with six noble allies and then spent a year putting down revolts across the empire, a campaign he had carved into the cliff at Behistun in three languages. He reorganised the realm into satrapies with fixed tribute, standardised coinage and law, built the Royal Road, and founded Persepolis.
nodes.src: Behistun Inscription (DB), trilingual Old Persian/Elamite/Babylonian; Herodotus, Histories 3.61–88, 3.89–97 (tribute list).

nodes.label: Truth and the Lie
nodes.full: Darius's inscription frames his year of civil war as a cosmic struggle between arta (truth/order) and drauga (the Lie) — every rebel is a 'Lie-follower' and Darius the restorer of truth under Ahura Mazda's favour, a legitimating formula repeated in later royal inscriptions across the dynasty.
nodes.src: Behistun Inscription (DB) §§4, 54–58, 63–69.

nodes.label: Behistun relief
nodes.full: Carved above the trilingual inscription, the relief shows Darius standing with his foot on the prostrate Gaumata while nine bound rebel kings await judgement before him — royal ideology rendered as image for an audience that could not read the cuneiform text beneath it.
nodes.src: Behistun relief and inscription (DB), in situ, Kermanshah Province, Iran.

nodes.label: Old Persian cuneiform
nodes.full: The Old Persian script used in Darius's Behistun inscription is a simplified, largely alphabetic cuneiform found nowhere before his reign — most specialists read it as a script created for this monument's ideological programme, distinct from the older syllabic Elamite and Babylonian cuneiforms carved alongside it.
nodes.src: Behistun Inscription (DB), Old Persian column; Roland Kent, Old Persian: Grammar, Texts, Lexicon (1953).

nodes.label: Ahura Mazda in royal ideology
nodes.full: Darius's tomb inscription at Naqsh-e Rustam declares Ahura Mazda the greatest of gods who made Darius king — but the same text also acknowledges 'the other gods who are', a formula that cautions against reading full Zoroastrian orthodoxy, as later codified under the Sasanians, back into Achaemenid royal religion.
nodes.src: Naqsh-e Rustam inscription of Darius I (DNa).

nodes.label: Democedes at court
nodes.full: A celebrated Greek physician from Croton, Democedes was brought to the Persian court as a captive, treated Darius's dislocated ankle and Queen Atossa's illness, and was retained at court with great honour before eventually escaping home — a documented individual case of Greek medical expertise crossing into Persian royal service.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 3.129–137.

nodes.label: Satrapy system
nodes.full: Darius I divided the empire into roughly twenty provinces (satrapies), each under a satrap balanced by an independent military commander and royal inspectors — the 'King's Eyes and Ears' — who reported directly to the throne, a structural check against provincial autonomy.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 3.89–97; Xenophon, Cyropaedia 8.6.16 (the King's Eyes).

nodes.label: Fixed tribute assessment
nodes.full: Herodotus preserves what appears to be an administrative document: a satrapy-by-satrap list of annual tribute owed in silver talents, from Ionia and Babylon's wealth down to Ethiopia's gold and India's gold dust — the earliest surviving imperial tax schedule from the ancient Near East.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 3.89–97.

nodes.label: Codification of Egyptian law
nodes.full: The Demotic Chronicle records that Darius I ordered Egyptian priests and officials to compile the country's laws 'down to year 44 of Amasis' into a single code — an act of governance through the deliberate patronage and continuity of a subject people's own legal tradition, not its replacement.
nodes.src: Demotic Chronicle (Papyrus Bibliothèque Nationale 215), verso; Hibis Temple dedication, Kharga Oasis.

nodes.label: The daric
nodes.full: Darius I reserved the minting of gold coin (the daric, named for him) as a royal monopoly, while satraps and cities could strike silver — a two-tier currency system that made gold coinage itself a symbol of Achaemenid sovereignty across the empire's Mediterranean-facing provinces.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 4.166; surviving daric specimens, British Museum and Cabinet des Médailles.

nodes.label: Law of the Medes and Persians
nodes.full: Later sources describe an Achaemenid legal principle that a king's sealed decree, once issued, could not be revoked even by the king himself — a constitutional constraint on royal power that appears in both the Book of Esther and the Book of Daniel as a narrative device reflecting a real administrative reputation.
nodes.src: Book of Esther 1:19, 8:8; Book of Daniel 6:8–15; Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 17.30.

nodes.label: Persepolis
nodes.full: Founded by Darius I as a ceremonial capital, Persepolis's terraced complex — the great audience hall (Apadana), the monumental Gate of All Nations, and the Hundred-Column Hall completed under Xerxes and Artaxerxes I — was built to stage the New Year's (Nowruz) reception of tribute from across the empire.
nodes.src: Persepolis Apadana foundation tablets (DPh, DPf); excavation reports, Oriental Institute of Chicago (Erich Schmidt, 1930s).

nodes.label: Apadana reliefs
nodes.full: The staircases of the Apadana carry processional reliefs of delegations from twenty-three subject peoples — Medes, Elamites, Babylonians, Egyptians, Indians, Scythians and others — each in distinct dress, bringing characteristic gifts, a visual encyclopaedia of imperial diversity staged as willing tribute.
nodes.src: Persepolis Apadana staircase reliefs, in situ; Walser, Die Völkerschaften auf den Reliefs von Persepolis (1966).

nodes.label: Rations and labour at Persepolis
nodes.full: Tens of thousands of Elamite tablets record grain, wine and livestock rations issued to work-gangs (kurtaš) of many nationalities building and provisioning Persepolis, including female supervisors paid at documented rates — a rare direct window onto the labour economy underpinning imperial construction.
nodes.src: Persepolis Fortification Archive; Richard Hallock, Persepolis Fortification Tablets (1969); Wouter Henkelman on female labour rations.

nodes.label: Royal women as estate-holders
nodes.full: Fortification tablets record women such as Irdabama and Irtaštuna (Artystone, a wife of Darius I) independently commanding large workforces, issuing rations under their own seals, and receiving allocations exceeding those of many male officials — direct administrative evidence of substantial female economic authority at the highest level of the empire.
nodes.src: Persepolis Fortification Archive; Maria Brosius, Women in Ancient Persia, 559–331 BC (1996).

nodes.label: Captive labour at Persepolis
nodes.full: Alongside paid specialist workers, the Fortification tablets describe gangs identified as war captives assigned to construction work at Persepolis — a labour force whose legal status sat somewhere between free wage-earner and the fully enslaved, a distinction the Achaemenid administrative vocabulary does not draw as sharply as later legal traditions.
nodes.src: Persepolis Fortification Archive; Pierre Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander: A History of the Persian Empire (2002), pp. 429–439.

nodes.label: Royal Road and angarium
nodes.full: A maintained highway of some 2,400 km linked Susa to Sardis with staging posts at regular intervals, along which relay riders of the angarium postal system could carry a royal message the length of the road in under a week — Herodotus's description of couriers undeterred by 'snow, rain, heat, or dark of night' describes this system.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 5.52–53, 8.98.

nodes.label: Royal Road as trade corridor
nodes.full: Beyond its administrative and military use, the Susa–Sardis highway and its connecting routes east to Bactria and India carried merchants, luxury goods and information across the length of the empire, prefiguring the corridor later trade networks would extend further into Central Asia.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 5.52–54; Xenophon, Cyropaedia 8.6.17–18 (on trade moving along maintained roads).

nodes.label: Scylax down the Indus
nodes.full: Darius I commissioned the Carian navigator Scylax of Caryanda to sail down the Indus and around the Arabian Peninsula to Egypt, mapping a sea route that fed directly into the annexation of the Indus valley as a satrapy and the completion of a Nile–Red Sea canal.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 4.44.

nodes.label: Darius Red Sea canal
nodes.full: Darius I completed a canal linking the Nile to the Red Sea, commemorated by a series of trilingual stelae along its route recording that ships sailed from Egypt to Persia through it — reopening and extending a waterway earlier Egyptian pharaohs had begun and abandoned.
nodes.src: Darius Suez Canal stelae (e.g. the Kabret/Chalouf stele, Egyptian Museum, Cairo and Louvre); Herodotus, Histories 2.158, 4.39.

nodes.label: Qanat irrigation
nodes.full: Underground gravity-fed qanat channels, tapping aquifers at the base of the Zagros and Alborz ranges and carrying water for kilometres without evaporation loss, expanded settled agriculture across the arid Iranian plateau and underwrote the tax base the satrapy system depended on.
nodes.src: Polybius, Histories 10.28 (on qanats in Media, describing an established technology); archaeological qanat surveys, Fars and Khorasan provinces.

nodes.label: Largest empire yet
nodes.full: At its territorial height under Darius I the empire stretched from Libya and Thrace in the west to the Indus valley in the east, and from the Caucasus to the Persian Gulf and southern Egypt — by most estimates the largest contiguous empire yet assembled, ruling a substantial share of the world's population.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 3.89–97 (satrapy list); Rein Taagepera, 'Size and Duration of Empires: Growth-Decline Curves, 600 B.C. to 600 A.D.' (1978).

nodes.label: Scythian campaign
nodes.full: Darius led an army across bridges of boats over the Bosphorus and then the Danube into European Scythia to punish nomadic raiders on the empire's northern frontier. The Scythians refused open battle and withdrew before him, and Darius eventually retreated without a decisive victory — the practical limit of Achaemenid expansion into the steppe.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 4.83–98, 4.118–142.

nodes.label: Garrison colonies
nodes.full: Persian frontier policy stationed permanent mixed garrisons — Jewish, Aramean, Caspian and Khwarezmian soldiers among them — at strategic points such as Elephantine on Egypt's southern border, granting land and communal autonomy to soldier-colonists in exchange for permanent military service.
nodes.src: Elephantine papyri (Cowley collection); Bezalel Porten, Archives from Elephantine (1968).

nodes.label: Imperial Aramaic
nodes.full: Aramaic, spread earlier by the Assyrian empire, became the Achaemenid chancery's working language from Egypt to Bactria — the Jewish military colony's archive at Elephantine and the satrap Arshama's own letters were both written in the same standardised administrative Aramaic, evidence of a genuinely empire-wide scribal culture.
nodes.src: Elephantine papyri (Brooklyn Museum, Berlin Museum); Bezalel Porten, Archives from Elephantine (1968).

nodes.label: Arshama letters
nodes.full: A cache of Aramaic letters from Arshama, the absentee Achaemenid satrap of Egypt, to his estate managers survives on leather — day-to-day instructions on runaway slaves, estate income and staff, giving an unusually intimate view of how a satrap actually governed at a distance.
nodes.src: Bodleian Library Aramaic Documents of Arshama; Tuplin & Ma (eds.), Aramaic Documents from Achaemenid Egypt (Oxford, 2020).

nodes.label: Arabian aromatics trade
nodes.full: Herodotus records Arabia as the sole Achaemenid tribute-payer to give frankincense rather than silver, a thousand talents a year, moving north along the incense route through Gaza — evidence that the empire taxed the aromatics trade in kind rather than displacing the merchant networks that ran it.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 3.97, 3.107–113.

nodes.label: Treasury reserve
nodes.full: Herodotus describes provincial silver tribute being melted into storage ingots at the royal treasuries rather than recoined and recirculated — a fiscal practice modern economic historians have linked to periodic silver shortages in the Aegean world that depended on Persian-controlled mining regions.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 3.96; Persepolis Treasury tablets, Oriental Institute of Chicago.

nodes.label: Murasu archive
nodes.full: The business archive of the Murašû banking family of Nippur records loans, land leases and tax-farming contracts with Persian officials and military fief-holders across three reigns — the fullest surviving picture of how Babylonian finance capital interlocked with imperial administration.
nodes.src: Murašû archive tablets, University of Pennsylvania Museum and Istanbul Archaeological Museum; Matthew Stolper, Entrepreneurs and Empire (1985).

nodes.label: Ionian Revolt
nodes.full: The Greek cities of Ionia, led by Miletus's Aristagoras and briefly aided by Athens and Eretria, rose against Persian-appointed tyrants and satrapal rule. Darius crushed the revolt at the naval Battle of Lade (494 BC) and the sack of Miletus, but Athens's involvement gave him his pretext for invading Greece.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 5.28–6.32.

nodes.label: Deportation of Eretria
nodes.full: After Eretria aided the Ionian Revolt, Darius's forces captured the city and deported its population to Ardericca, a settlement near Susa, where Herodotus reports their descendants still lived generations later — forced resettlement used as both punishment and a means of populating the imperial heartland.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 6.119.

nodes.label: Greco-Persian Wars
nodes.full: Darius's punitive expedition was stopped at Marathon in 490 BC; Xerxes's far larger invasion a decade later forced the pass at Thermopylae and burned Athens, but lost its fleet at Salamis (480 BC) and its army at Plataea (479 BC), ending Persia's attempts to conquer the Greek mainland.

nodes.label: Xerxes I
nodes.full: Xerxes suppressed revolts in Egypt and Babylon early in his reign, then led a massive invasion of Greece in 480 BC — forcing Thermopylae, burning Athens, and losing the fleet at Salamis before withdrawing. He completed Persepolis's Gate of All Nations and was assassinated in a palace conspiracy in 465 BC.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 7–9; Persepolis Gate of All Nations trilingual inscription (XPa).

nodes.label: Babylon demoted
nodes.full: After Babylon revolted twice early in Xerxes's reign, Persian forces suppressed the uprisings and later classical tradition holds that the golden statue of Marduk was removed and the city's special satrapal status downgraded — imperial reprisal falling on a population whose earlier cooperation Cyrus's own propaganda had once celebrated.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 1.183 (on the statue, from an earlier visit); Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 7.17 (on Xerxes, a later tradition treated cautiously by modern historians).

nodes.label: Atossa and Parysatis
nodes.full: Herodotus credits Queen Atossa with decisively urging Darius toward the invasion of Greece; two generations later Parysatis backed her favourite son Cyrus the Younger's rebellion against his brother Artaxerxes II with money and influence — two documented instances of queens shaping high policy from within the court rather than through formal office.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories 3.134; Plutarch, Life of Artaxerxes 2, 6, 19.

nodes.label: Herodotus
nodes.full: Herodotus of Halicarnassus, himself a subject of the Persian empire by birth, composed the first extended narrative history of the Greek world's conflict with Persia — the dominant external source for Achaemenid political history, valuable and frequently unreliable in the same passages, and read against Persian inscriptions wherever they survive.
nodes.src: Herodotus, Histories, esp. books 1, 3, 7–9.

nodes.label: Artaxerxes I
nodes.full: After the chiliarch Artabanus murdered Xerxes and moved to seize power, Xerxes's son Artaxerxes overthrew and killed him — also killing his own brother Darius, accused of the assassination, to secure the throne. His long reign saw the loss and reconquest of Egypt and, by tradition, a peace settlement with Athens.
nodes.src: Ctesias, Persica (via Photius); Thucydides 1.104, 1.109–110 (the Egyptian revolt).

nodes.label: Inaros revolt
nodes.full: The Libyan prince Inaros led Egypt in revolt against Artaxerxes I with a large Athenian naval expeditionary force in support, defeating a Persian army at Papremis before the revolt was finally crushed and Inaros executed at Susa.
nodes.src: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 1.104, 1.109–110; Ctesias, Persica (via Photius).

nodes.label: Peace of Callias
nodes.full: Greek tradition held that an Athenian embassy under Callias negotiated a settlement with Artaxerxes I ending large-scale hostilities between Persia and the Delian League — the treaty's exact terms and even its historicity are debated in the ancient sources themselves, a live problem for historians rather than a settled fact.
nodes.src: Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 12.4; Plutarch, Life of Cimon 13 (recording ancient doubts about the treaty's authenticity).

nodes.label: Nehemiah mission
nodes.full: Nehemiah, a cupbearer at Artaxerxes I's court, obtained royal authorisation and letters of safe passage to rebuild Jerusalem's walls — an unusually detailed first-person Judean account of how a subject community secured and used imperial favour.
nodes.src: Book of Nehemiah 1–6.

nodes.label: Xerxes II
nodes.full: The only son of Artaxerxes I born to a legitimate queen, Xerxes II held the throne for barely six weeks before being murdered in his sleep by his half-brother Sogdianus — the opening act of a succession crisis that would burn through three kings in a single year.
nodes.src: Ctesias, Persica (via Photius, Bibliotheca 72).

nodes.label: Sogdianus
nodes.full: Sogdianus, son of a royal concubine, seized the throne by murdering his half-brother Xerxes II, then held it for barely half a year before another half-brother, Ochus — satrap of Hyrcania — marched on Susa and overthrew him in turn.
nodes.src: Ctesias, Persica (via Photius, Bibliotheca 72).

nodes.label: Darius II
nodes.full: Ochus took the throne name Darius II after defeating Sogdianus. His queen Parysatis exercised major influence at court, and in the closing years of the Peloponnesian War his satraps funnelled Persian gold to Sparta's fleet, tipping the balance against Athens.
nodes.src: Xenophon, Hellenica 1–2; Thucydides 8 (Persian-Spartan negotiations).

nodes.label: Subsidy of Sparta
nodes.full: Darius II's satraps Tissaphernes and, later, the crown prince Cyrus the Younger financed the Spartan war effort against Athens in exchange for a free hand over the Greek cities of Asia Minor — Persian gold that proved decisive in Athens's final naval defeat.
nodes.src: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 8.5–6, 8.18 (the treaties with Sparta); Xenophon, Hellenica 1–2.

nodes.label: Cunaxa and the Ten Thousand
nodes.full: Cyrus the Younger marched a Persian and Greek mercenary army against his brother Artaxerxes II, dying in the moment of near-victory at Cunaxa. The stranded Greek mercenaries' fighting retreat north to the Black Sea, chronicled by Xenophon, exposed the empire's western vulnerability a generation before Alexander.
nodes.src: Xenophon, Anabasis, books 1–4.

nodes.label: Artaxerxes II
nodes.full: Artaxerxes survived his younger brother Cyrus the Younger's rebellion in the first years of his reign, held the throne for 46 years — the longest of any Achaemenid king — and dictated the terms of Greek interstate politics through the King's Peace of 387 BC after losing Egypt to a successful native revolt.
nodes.src: Xenophon, Anabasis 1; Xenophon, Hellenica 5.1.31 (the King's Peace).

nodes.label: Artaxerxes III
nodes.full: Later Greek tradition accuses Artaxerxes III of executing rival relatives to secure his succession. He reconquered Egypt in 343 BC, ending the last native Egyptian dynasty, before being poisoned by his own chiliarch, the eunuch Bagoas.
nodes.src: Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 16.40–51 (the Egyptian campaign), 17.5 (the poisoning).

nodes.label: Arses
nodes.full: Bagoas installed the young Arses after poisoning Artaxerxes III and most other claimants to the throne. When Arses tried to act against him, Bagoas poisoned him too, after barely two years on the throne.
nodes.src: Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 17.5.

nodes.label: Eunuchs of the court
nodes.full: Greek sources describe eunuchs holding senior military and administrative posts at court, most dramatically Bagoas, who by their account made and unmade two kings in succession. This is evidence of a court institution of real political power; later writers' hostile framing of the individuals involved should not be mistaken for a claim about inner identity the sources never make.
nodes.src: Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 17.5; Curtius Rufus, Historiae Alexandri Magni 6.5.23.

nodes.label: Darius III
nodes.full: A collateral descendant of the royal line, Darius III was raised to the throne by Bagoas and promptly forced the kingmaker to drink his own poison. He lost the empire to Alexander's invasion across three pitched battles and was murdered by his own satrap Bessus in Bactria in 330 BC.
nodes.src: Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 17.5–6, 17.73 (the murder by Bessus); Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 3.21.

nodes.label: Alexander conquest
nodes.full: Alexander defeated Darius III in three pitched battles — the Granicus (334 BC), Issus (333 BC), and the decisive Gaugamela (331 BC) — before occupying Babylon, Susa and Persepolis and pursuing the fleeing king into Bactria, where Darius was murdered by his own satrap Bessus.
nodes.src: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 1–3; Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 17.

nodes.label: Fall of the empire
nodes.full: With Darius III murdered by his own satrap Bessus in Bactria, two centuries of Achaemenid rule ended. Alexander proclaimed himself Darius's avenger and heir, and the imperial structure the Achaemenids had built — the satrapies, the Royal Road, the chancery Aramaic — passed largely intact into Hellenistic hands.
nodes.src: Arrian, Anabasis of Alexander 3.21–22; Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica 17.73.
